title: Your Insecure MCP Server Won't Survive Production — Tun Shwe, Lenses

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 93%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is MCP protocol security, OAuth 2.1 integration, and tool-calling contract design for production agent systems. Security and defense is central via prompt injection, confused deputy vulnerabilities, RBAC, and governance; developer platforms applies as MCP is infrastructure other engineers build on. The talk addresses moving MCP servers from local development into production deployment with enterprise-grade security layers. Advanced prerequisites include OAuth flows, MCP familiarity, and API security concepts, plus 10+ RFC specifications referenced. This is a conference talk presented at AI Engineer by Lenses.io engineers. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting evidence anchors.

summary:
Tun Shwe and Jeremy Frenay from Lenses.io argue that MCP server design and security are inseparable disciplines. They frame three dimensions where agents differ from humans—discovery, iteration, and context—each casting a security shadow. Discovery: agents enumerate all tools and descriptions every connection, expanding the surface for tool poisoning. Iteration: agents resend full conversation history on retries, risking data leakage. Context: dumping unfiltered data into a limited token window creates opportunities for context injection and oversharing per OWASP MCP Top 10.

They propose five principles for secure agentic design: (1) shrink the attack surface by consolidating fine-grained operations into coarse-grained outcome-based tools; (2) constrain inputs at the schema level using primitives, enums, and Pydantic; (3) treat documentation as a defensive layer against tool poisoning; (4) return only what the agent needs, stripping PII and credentials; (5) minimize blast radius by scoping permissions at tool/resource level, using read-only annotations and converting read-only tools to MCP resources.

They describe the security cliff: local stdio mode needs no auth but fails under concurrency (Stacklok tests showed 20 of 22 requests failed with 20 simultaneous connections), forcing a move to streamable HTTP for production. There is no gradual on-ramp—teams need OAuth, TLS, CORS, and rate limiting simultaneously. Long-lived, unscoped, shared API keys create confused deputy vulnerabilities.

Jeremy then covers OAuth 2.1 in detail. Traditional pre-registration breaks because MCP has unbounded clients connecting to unbounded servers. Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) allows self-registration but has problems: registrations are non-portable across devices, it is vulnerable to phishing since anyone can post to the register endpoint, and servers must trust self-asserted client metadata. The MCP community developed CIMD (Client ID Metadata Document) as a better approach: clients expose their metadata at a public URL, the authorization server fetches it during authorization, eliminating the registration database, binding redirect URIs explicitly, and allowing selective client allow/deny. CIMD has been the preferred approach since November 2025. The full OAuth flow uses PKCE, token exchange (RFC 8693) for least-privilege session tokens, and JWT access tokens.

Beyond OAuth, enterprise-grade MCP requires tool-level RBAC (not just session-level scopes), data masking for PII before agents see it, audit logging of which agent called which tool with what parameters and results, and end-to-end observability for compliance with regulations like the EU AI Act.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Lenses.io Context
sections.summary: Tun Shwe and Jeremy Frenay introduce themselves as AI engineers at Lenses.io, a data operating fabric providing trusted real-time context to agentic AI with governance, security, and large scale. They have an open source MCP server on GitHub and will cover design principles for robust MCP servers and securing MCP services for production.

sections.title: Why Most MCP Servers Aren't Great: Security Shadows
sections.summary: Three dimensions where agents differ from humans each cast a security shadow. Discovery: agents enumerate all tools each connection, expanding tool poisoning surface. Iteration: agents resend full conversation history on retries, risking data leakage. Context: limited token windows make unfiltered data a context injection and oversharing risk per OWASP MCP Top 10. Curation and minimal exposure are recommended.

sections.title: Five Key Rules for Secure Agentic Design
sections.summary: Five principles: (1) shrink attack surface by consolidating into coarse-grained outcome-based tools; (2) constrain inputs at schema level with enums, primitives, and Pydantic; (3) treat documentation as defensive layer against tool poisoning; (4) return only essential data to avoid context window liability; (5) minimize blast radius with tool-level permissions, read-only annotations, and resource conversion. Every tool removed eliminates an attack vector.

sections.title: The Security Cliff: Local to Production
sections.summary: Local stdio mode is comfortable but single-user with no network exposure. Production requires streamable HTTP transport for remote deployment, multiple clients, scaling, and centralized governance. There is no gradual on-ramp—teams need OAuth, token management, CORS, TLS, and rate limiting all at once. Stacklok tests showed stdio fails badly under concurrency: 20 of 22 requests failed with 20 simultaneous connections.

sections.title: OAuth Flows: Local vs Remote MCP Server Setups
sections.summary: Jeremy covers OAuth implementation complexity (10+ RFCs). Local setup: API key stored as environment variable, passed to external service, long-lived and rarely rotated. Remote setup: API key in HTTP authorization header, may or may not be validated by MCP server, often passed through to upstream API. Both approaches use long-lived, unscoped keys. Remote shared credentials create confused deputy vulnerabilities, are harder to revoke per user, and compromise everyone if leaked.

sections.title: Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) Flow
sections.summary: Traditional OAuth pre-registration breaks for MCP because unbounded clients connect to unbounded servers at runtime. DCR allows clients to self-register against the authorization server. The full flow: client discovers MCP server via 401 with WWW-Authenticate header containing resource metadata, self-registers via POST /register to get a new client ID, authorizes using PKCE through /authorize, user authenticates at identity provider and grants scopes on consent page, client exchanges authorization code for JWT access token at /token, MCP server validates token and performs token exchange (RFC 8693) to obtain a session token for the upstream API.

sections.title: DCR Limitations and CIMD Approach
sections.summary: DCR has problems: each client connection creates a new non-portable registration (using Claude on Windows and macOS creates two distinct registrations), it is vulnerable to phishing since anyone can post to /register, and servers must trust self-asserted client metadata. CIMD (Client ID Metadata Document) solves these: client owners expose client metadata at a public URL, the authorization server fetches it during /authorize, eliminating the registration database, binding redirect URIs explicitly to the client, and enabling selective client allow/deny. CIMD has been the preferred approach since November 2025.

sections.title: Enterprise-Grade Security Layers
sections.summary: Beyond OAuth, enterprise-grade MCP requires: tool-level RBAC (OAuth scopes are session-level only, insufficient for individual tool and resource permissions); data masking for PII fields before agents see them; audit logging of which agent called which tool with what parameters and returned data for EU AI Act compliance; and end-to-end observability tracing from client request through execution, data retrieval, and generated response. If you cannot trace what an agent did end to end, you cannot govern it. Tun closes by inviting feedback and pointing to their open source MCP server on GitHub.

demonstrations: Flow diagram of local MCP server: server runs locally via standard IO, client connects with API key stored as environment variable in MCP client config, key passed through to external service

Flow diagram of remote MCP server: server runs remotely, client connects via HTTP, API key set in authorization header, key may or may not be validated by MCP server before pass-through to upstream API

DCR flow diagram: client discovers MCP server via 401 with WWW-Authenticate header, self-registers via POST /register obtaining client ID, authorizes via PKCE through /authorize, user logs in at identity provider and grants scopes, client exchanges authorization code for JWT access token at /token, MCP server performs token exchange (RFC 8693) for session token before API call

CIMD flow diagram: client discovers MCP server via 401 and resource metadata URL, skips /register, passes unique ID (public URL) in /authorize request, authorization server fetches client metadata from that URL, registers client with URL-based unique ID, proceeds to authentication and token issuance
